root_claim: A misplaced decimal point made spinach famous as an iron-rich food.
conclusion: The overstated iron figure for spinach was reproduced in food composition tables, textbooks, and popular media for decades before being corrected.
premises: Published analyses of spinach iron content in the early twentieth century reported a value of roughly 35 mg of iron per 100 g of spinach.
The true iron content of fresh spinach is approximately 2–4 mg per 100 g, about one tenth of 35 mg per 100 g.
National and institutional food composition tables published across multiple decades listed spinach iron values of the order of tens of milligrams per 100 g.
Nutrition and dietetics textbooks repeated the elevated spinach iron figure taken from food composition tables in successive editions.
Newspapers, magazines, and cartoons promoted spinach as an exceptionally iron-rich food during the same period in which the elevated figure circulated in reference works.
A published correction identifying the spinach iron value as roughly tenfold too high appeared at least several decades after the erroneous figure first entered reference works.

A figure appearing continuously in reference tables, teaching texts, and mass-market publications over a span exceeding twenty years, and only afterwards revised, counts as having been reproduced for decades before being corrected.

root_claim: Listening to Mozart raises a child's IQ.
conclusion: The post-listening cognitive gains attributed to Mozart are not fully explained by general arousal, mood elevation, or practice effects that any preferred stimulus would produce.
premises: Listening to a Mozart sonata produces a measurable short-term improvement on spatial-temporal reasoning tasks relative to a silence or relaxation-instruction control condition.

In experiments comparing a Mozart excerpt against a non-musical or non-preferred auditory stimulus matched for arousal level, the Mozart condition yields higher spatial-task scores than the matched-arousal condition.

Studies that measure mood and arousal alongside spatial-task performance after music listening find that statistically controlling for mood and arousal does not eliminate the performance advantage of the Mozart condition.

Experimental designs for the Mozart effect that use different spatial-task items at each testing session, or counterbalance task order across conditions, remove repeated-exposure practice as an explanation for score differences between conditions.
Listener-preference-matched control stimuli, in which each participant hears a self-selected preferred piece instead of Mozart, do not produce cognitive gains equal to those of the Mozart condition.
Arousal, mood elevation, and practice effects are the principal non-music-specific mechanisms proposed to account for post-listening cognitive test gains.
